w: Built between 1598 and 1629, this maidan is big enough to lose track of its own edges -- 160 by 560 meters, ringed by a mosque, a palace, another mosque, and the gate into the Grand Bazaar, each facing the square from its own side. It appears on the 20,000 rial note; in Isfahan, it simply is the center.
s: The square so big it is on the banknote
_facts: constructed 1598-1629, 160m by 560m, about 89,600 square meters, UNESCO World Heritage Site
surrounded by Safavid-era buildings: Shah Mosque (south), Ali Qapu Palace (west), Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque (east), Qeysarie Gate into the Grand Bazaar (north)
known as Shah Square before 1979, sometimes Imam Square; depicted on the 20,000 Iranian rial banknote

w: Sixteen years in the building, this mosque skips the usual minaret and courtyard -- an unusual, private commission from Shah Abbas the Great, its dome patterned in cream and blue that seems to shift color through the day. American scholar Arthur Upham Pope talked a later shah into restoring it in the 1920s.
s: The mosque with no minaret, built for a shah alone
_facts: construction started 1602/03 CE, finished 1618/19 CE, designed by chief architect Muhammad Reza under Shah Abbas the Great
one of the masterpieces of Iranian architecture from the Safavid era, on the eastern side of Naqsh-e Jahan Square
restored in the 1920s by Reza Shah Pahlavi on the advice of Arthur Upham Pope
UNESCO World Heritage Site alongside the square

w: Officially the Imam Mosque now, everyone still calls this the Shah Mosque -- Abbas the Great's grandest commission, roughly nineteen years in construction, closing the south end of the maidan it shares with a palace and a private mosque. It is the one still holding Friday prayers, same as four centuries ago.
_facts: construction began 1611, completed around 1630, ordered by Shah Abbas the Great
officially known as the Imam Mosque or Imam Khomeini Mosque, on the south side of Naqsh-e Jahan Square
regarded as a masterpiece of Persian Islamic architecture, UNESCO World Heritage Site
Friday prayers still held here; depicted on the 20,000 rial banknote

w: Six floors up a punishing spiral staircase sits the Music Hall, its walls carved with deep niches doubling as decoration and acoustic tuning. Shah Abbas the Great used this palace gate to entertain ambassadors and celebrate Nowruz here, back when it was the grand entrance to a palace reaching to Chaharbagh.
s: A palace gate with a music hall on top
_facts: imperial palace on the western side of Naqsh-e Jahan Square, built early 17th century under Shah Abbas the Great
48 meters high, six floors reached by a spiral staircase; the sixth-floor Music Hall has circular wall niches valued for acoustics and aesthetics
originally the grand portal entrance to a palace complex stretching to Chaharbagh Boulevard, used to entertain ambassadors and celebrate Nowruz
regarded as the best example of Safavid architecture, decorated with naturalistic wall paintings

w: Twelve centuries of continuous renovation, starting around 771 CE, have left this mosque as something like a layered core sample of Islamic architecture in Iran -- each era from the Abbasids to the Safavids adding its own wing. The Grand Bazaar spills out from its southwest corner. UNESCO listed it in 2012.
_facts: also known as the Atiq Mosque or Friday Mosque, result of continual construction and renovation from c.771 CE to the end of the 20th century
the Grand Bazaar of Isfahan lies toward its southwest wing
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012
one of the largest and most important monuments of Islamic architecture in Iran

w: Thirty-three arches carry this bridge across the Zayanderud -- officially the Allahverdi Khan Bridge, built in the early 1600s to work as both crossing and dam. It is the largest of Isfahan's eleven historic river bridges, and still the one everyone means when they just say 'the bridge.'
s: 33 arches, doing double duty as a dam
_facts: officially the Allahverdi Khan Bridge, popularly Si-o-se-pol meaning 'bridge of thirty-three spans'
the largest of eleven historical bridges on the Zayanderud, the largest river of the Iranian Plateau
built in the early 17th century to serve as both bridge and dam

w: Isfahan's finest bridge, by most accounts, doubles as a weir and once served as a public meeting hall -- linking the Khaju quarter to the old Zoroastrian district across the water. Two American scholars who fell for Persian art, Arthur Upham Pope and Phyllis Ackerman, are buried in a mausoleum beside it.
_facts: historic bridge on the Zayanderud, serving as both bridge and weir
links the Khaju quarter on the north bank with the Zoroastrian quarter across the river
served as a building and place for public meetings historically, described as the city's finest bridge
art historians Arthur Upham Pope and Phyllis Ackerman are interred in a mausoleum nearby

w: Sasanian engineers laid the foundations of this bridge some 1,500 years ago; Buyid and Seljuk builders added the arches later. It bends westward against the current, built from 13 large arches and 8 smaller nested ones. The river has since been diverted, leaving the bridge over an artificial lake for protection.
s: Isfahan's oldest bridge, engineered to bend water
_facts: the oldest bridge on the Zayandeh River, foundations date to the Sasanian era (224-651 CE), renovated by Buyids in the 10th century and Seljuks in the 11th
two-parabola design: a vertical parabola for the highest midpoint, a horizontal parabola bending west against the river flow
13 large pointed arches spanning the river plus 8 smaller nested arches, 107.8 meters long
the Zayandeh River has been diverted about 100 meters away, leaving an artificial lake around the bridge for protection

w: Officially the Holy Savior Cathedral, everyone calls this the Vank -- Armenian for 'monastery' -- the spiritual heart of the New Julfa district's Armenian Apostolic community, also known as the Church of the Saintly Sisters.
s: New Julfa's Armenian cathedral, called the Vank
_facts: officially the Holy Savior Cathedral, also known as the Church of the Saintly Sisters
an Armenian Apostolic cathedral located in the New Julfa district of Isfahan
commonly referred to as the Vank, meaning monastery or convent in Armenian

w: Shake one of these two minarets by hand and the other sways in sympathy -- a structural quirk built into a shrine over the grave of Sufi ascetic Amu Abdullah Suqla. Construction started under the Ilkhanids and finished under the Safavids; the shaking trick has outlasted both dynasties.
s: Shake one minaret, the other one moves
_facts: Persian name means 'Shaking minarets', a mosque and mausoleum built over the grave of Sufi ascetic Amu Abdullah Suqla
construction started in the Ilkhanate era and finished during the Safavid era
the two minarets both shake and sway when one of them is shaken
added to the Iran National Heritage List on 10 June 1942

w: Commissioned by Shah Soltan Hoseyn in the twilight of Safavid rule, this theological school still carries its old nickname -- Madrese-ye Madar-e Shah, the Shah's Mother's School. Isfahan's grandest religious college, built to train clergy in the empire's final, most ornate decades.
s: The Shah's Mother's School, in tile and marble
_facts: also known as Chahar Bagh School or Madrese-ye Madar-e Shah, a 17th-18th century cultural complex
built in the late Safavid era under the reign of Shah Soltan Hoseyn
served as a theological and clerical school

w: Shah Suleiman I built this pavilion as a private retreat and called it Hasht Behesht -- the Eight Heavens. Centuries later it picked up an unlikely second life as His Majesty's School, Isfahan's first modern school, tucked inside the same royal garden on Chaharbagh Street.
s: The Eight Heavens, later a school
_facts: 17th-century pavilion built by order of Suleiman I, eighth shah of Safavid Iran, functioned mainly as a private pavilion
located on Isfahan's Chaharbagh Street
also served as the first modern school in Isfahan, called His Majesty's School (Madrese-ye Homayouni)

w: Built as a Safavid-era caravanserai to shelter travelers, this complex spent centuries as a waystation before a French archaeologist talked Isfahan into restoring it as a hotel. Oliver Reed and Elke Sommer checked in for real in 1974, when the murder-mystery film And Then There Were None shot its scenes inside.
s: A Safavid caravanserai turned film set
_facts: formerly the Shah Abbas Hotel, the whole complex built during the reign of Sultan Husayn of Safavid Iran to provide lodging for travelers
French archaeologist Andre Godard suggested renovating the caravanserai; the Cultural Heritage Organization of Isfahan proceeded with the work
the 1974 film And Then There Were None, starring Oliver Reed and Elke Sommer, was shot here

w: This Sasanian-era complex sits atop a hill that rises 210 meters over the plain west of the city, once known as Maras or Marabin before Arab historians settled on the name that stuck. A pre-Islamic fire temple, still standing above everything around it.
s: A pre-Islamic fire temple on a 210m hill
_facts: the Fire Temple of Isfahan is a Sasanian-era archaeological complex on a hill about 8 kilometers west of Isfahan's city center
the hill rises about 210 meters above the surrounding plain, previously called Maras or Marabin
referred to by that name by Arab historians

w: The Nizari Ismailis held this fortress until Seljuk sultan Muhammad Tapar's campaign against them tore it down for good. What's left is a scatter of picturesque ruins on a spur of Mount Soffeh, eight kilometers south of the city -- a lost stronghold from a real medieval power struggle.
s: A destroyed Ismaili stronghold on Mount Soffeh
_facts: also called Dizkuh, a fortress near Isfahan notably held by the Nizari Ismailis
captured and destroyed in Seljuk sultan Muhammad Tapar's anti-Nizari campaign
conspicuous, picturesque ruins lie about 8 km south of Isfahan on a subpeak of Mount Soffeh

w: Here lies Saib Tabrizi, one of 17th-century Iran's most celebrated poets, in a mausoleum that has been on the national heritage list since 1977. No grand claims beyond that -- just a poet's grave, still visited for the words rather than the architecture.
s: The grave of a 17th-century master poet
_facts: Islamic mausoleum, burial place of Mohammad Ali ibn Mirza Abdul Rahim Tabrizi, known as Saib Tabrizi, a famous 17th century Iranian poet
added to the Iran National Heritage List on 9 February 1977

w: Three thousand-plus Safavid and Qajar pieces fill a building that started life as part of Shah Abbas I's Charbagh Palace. Next door stands a plain Qajar-era tower with a rough resume of its own -- watchtower first, then a jail -- undecorated but still counted among the city's notable Safavid relics.
s: Decorative arts beside a former jail tower
_facts: founded 1995, more than 3000 artworks from the Safavid and Qajar eras
building constructed during the reign of Abbas I as part of the Charbagh Palace
a Qajar-era multi-storey tower beside the museum was originally a watchtower, later a jail, regarded as a notable relic of Safavid architecture

w: Built in the 17th century as the grand entrance to Isfahan's Grand Bazaar, this gate used to have a third floor -- a naqqarekhane, or drum house, where musicians once announced the hour. That floor is long gone, but the gate still funnels the bazaar's daily crowds through the same Safavid archway.
s: The bazaar's gate, minus its drum house
_facts: historic gate at the main entrance of the Grand Bazaar (Qeysarie Bazaar) of Isfahan
originally had three floors; the destroyed third floor was a naqqarekhane (drum house)
built in the 17th century during the Safavid era
